title: Following Guyanese Gold: Crime, Power, and Illicit Flows
summary: Maya and Daniel examine a major investigation by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime and SWISSAID into Guyana's gold sector. They explore how elite capture, under-declaration, cross-border smuggling, and international trading hubs like the UAE fuel illicit financial flows across South America and beyond.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Welcome to the podcast. Today we're diving into a brand new investigation titled Following Guyanese Gold: Illicit Gold and Financial Flows in Guyana, published jointly by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime and SWISSAID.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And if you follow illicit finance, commodity smuggling, or Latin American security, this report is essential reading. Guyana is often in the headlines these days because of its offshore oil boom, but gold has historically been its economic backbone.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly. From the late 1990s all the way to 2019, gold was Guyana's single largest earner of foreign exchange. And even today, artisanal and small-scale gold mining accounts for up to 88 percent of national production, employing between 17,000 and 35,000 people. But what GI-TOC and SWISSAID uncover is a sector deeply captured by political elites, hollowed out by systematic under-declaration, and linked to transnational organized crime.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Right, and let's jump straight to one of the most glaring data points in the report. Over the last few years, global gold prices have soared to record highs. Usually, when gold prices skyrocket, you expect declared exports to surge. But in Guyana, official numbers did the exact opposite.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: They cratered. Total declared production reported by the Bank of Guyana fell by 32 percent between 2019 and 2024, dropping from 19.7 tonnes down to 13.5 tonnes. The central bank blamed things like bad weather and labour shortages.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Which sounds plausible on the surface if you have heavy rains flooding pit mines, but the researchers interviewed more than 30 people across the sector, and they paint a completely different picture, don't they?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Totally different. Nine sector insiders independently estimated that official declarations represent only about half of actual output. Smuggling by traders and dealers is the real driver. In fact, Guyana's own Financial Intelligence Unit flagged this in suspicious transaction reports back in 2023.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And when SWISSAID looked at mirror trade statistics, comparing what Guyana said it exported against what destination countries reported importing, the numbers didn't line up at all.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Between 2018 and 2024, the United Arab Emirates reported importing 12.6 tonnes more Guyanese gold than Guyana reported exporting to the UAE. That is 12.6 tonnes of gold that apparently left Guyana completely off the books.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: That is an astonishing discrepancy. And there was another odd mismatch with Belgium in 2024, right?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Yes, Guyana reported exporting 2.3 tonnes of gold to Belgium in 2024, but Belgium only recorded receiving 0.5 tonnes. The report notes this could indicate reporting errors, deliberate mislabelling, or gold being diverted and smuggled to an entirely different country.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: So how does a gap of this magnitude happen? What does the domestic setup look like on the ground that allows so much gold to vanish?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It comes down to elite capture and a concept locals refer to as 'friends, family and favourites'. For decades across successive administrations, power, politics, and gold have been tightly intertwined. Look at the mining concessions: GYEITI data from 2023 shows that just five individuals controlled over 65 percent of the surface area of all mining claims.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: 65 percent held by five people. That is extreme concentration.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It leads to widespread landlordism. Powerful claim holders don't necessarily mine the ground themselves. Instead, they act as rentiers, informally leasing out land to tribute miners, known locally as tributors, often for cash or demanding a fixed cut, like five ounces of gold a month or 10 percent of production. These tributors have zero tenure security, shoulder all the exploration risks, and get evicted the moment they hit a rich vein.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the regulator that is supposed to supervise all this, the Guyana Geology and Mines Commission, or GGMC, seems structurally compromised.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Severely compromised. The prominent industry lobby, the Guyana Gold and Diamond Miners Association, or GGDMA, exerts huge influence over the GGMC. Three GGDMA members sit on the GGMC board. In fact, one prominent family in GGDMA leadership includes the country's largest dredge owner by licences, the single largest gold mining permit holder, and the third-largest claim holder by area.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And when it comes to basic regulatory oversight, the GGMC has essentially operated on archaic paper-based systems. Concession tenure data hasn't been updated online since 2022 and completely excludes small-scale mining. The report also highlights that the GGMC's last audited financial statements date back to 2017, even though by 2023 its draft accounts showed it sitting on over 23 billion Guyanese dollars in cash.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: That's over 70 million US dollars. Meanwhile, environmental reclamation bonds paid by miners aren't tracked transparently, and clean-up spending is charged against general revenue instead of those bonds. When civil society groups try to question this, they face intimidation, break-ins, and public smears from government officials. Even the local Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative chapter, GYEITI, was thrown into crisis when the government appointed private sector figures, including an active gold miner, to convene the civil society pillar.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: That directly violates international EITI standards on civil society independence. Now, let's talk about the major players in the gold trade itself, because the report focuses heavily on a culture of impunity surrounding the two dominant buying and exporting firms: Mohamed's Enterprise and El Dorado Trading.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Right. Nazar 'Shell' Mohamed and his son Azruddin Mohamed ran Mohamed's Enterprise. In June 2024, the US Treasury Department sanctioned both men for public corruption. Then in October 2025, a federal grand jury in Miami indicted them in connection with a multi-year scheme to evade over 50 million dollars in taxes and royalties through fraudulent export declarations and money laundering.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And what did Guyanese authorities do prior to that US indictment?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Essentially nothing. Despite years of red flags and intelligence from foreign law enforcement, Guyanese authorities never brought domestic charges. In fact, the Mohameds long enjoyed close political ties with the ruling party. Interestingly, the political rift only deepened when Azruddin Mohamed launched his own political party, We Invest in Nationhood, in early 2025, won 16 parliamentary seats, and became leader of the opposition in January 2026. Both men were arrested for extradition in late 2025, released on bail, and are fighting extradition in the Guyanese courts.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And what about the other giant exporter, El Dorado Trading, founded by Tamesh Jagmohan?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: El Dorado faced allegations back in 2020 that it was sourcing illicit Venezuelan gold tied to armed groups. That prompted the Royal Canadian Mint to suspend refining gold from El Dorado. Jagmohan vehemently denied the allegations and no charges were ever brought. But the report points out that the domestic inquiries went nowhere, and the Gold Board reviewing the matter was actively purchasing El Dorado's gold to sell to the Royal Canadian Mint. In early 2022, Jagmohan asked the home affairs minister for an investigation to get a clean bill of health, and just weeks later, he and his brother donated ten vehicles to the police force, handed directly to that same minister.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: <laugh> The optics on that are incredible. The report also mentions past transactions between El Dorado and entities in Antwerp tied to the Goetz family, who were convicted of money laundering in Belgium in 2020.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Exactly, raising persistent questions about links to high-risk foreign intermediaries.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Let's turn to the regional dynamics, because one of the most fascinating findings in this report is what's happening along the borders with Brazil and Venezuela. Historically, the flow went into Guyana, right? Gold from Venezuela or Brazil was smuggled into Guyana to be laundered.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: That was the traditional pattern. But the report reveals a major inversion: gold is now being smuggled out of Guyana, through Brazil, and into Venezuela. In 2023, Brazilian President Lula evicted around 20,000 illegal miners from Yanomami Indigenous territory in Roraima. Many of those miners and their heavy machinery simply shifted across the border into Guyana, especially around Marudi Mountain in the south.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And the figures showing up at Marudi Mountain are notorious. The South Rupununi District Council identified Rodrigo Martins de Mello, known as Rodrigo Cataratas, as an investor in the area.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Yes! Cataratas was under Brazilian Federal Police investigation for years for running illegal mining logistics in Yanomami territory. In January 2026, he was convicted at first instance in Brazil and sentenced to over 22 years of detention and imprisonment, though his lawyers appealed and maintain his innocence. Yet he moved heavy machinery, including a 90-tonne excavator, into Guyana and partnered with local mining associations. Brazilian federal prosecutors also confirmed that the Macedo brothers, who were previously arrested in Brazil's Operation Ganância, shifted their primary mining operations to Marudi Mountain.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And where does that gold go? Locals at Marudi say the vast majority is smuggled right across the border to Boa Vista, Brazil. And from Boa Vista, it heads straight into Venezuela.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Boa Vista has become the central logistical turntable. It's about 100 kilometres from both Guyana and Venezuela, and private flights arriving at Boa Vista International Airport reportedly don't have their luggage scanned. Illicit gold is melted into bars in local foundries, often reaching 98 percent purity. Then trafficking networks smuggle it up to Las Claritas in Venezuela, where Venezuelan military generals buy it at an 8 percent premium above international market prices.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Paying 8 percent above world spot price! That explains why the flow reversed. But how are these cross-border deals financed? Are they moving suitcases of physical cash?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Sometimes cash, but the report documents a very modern mechanism: cryptocurrency. Two sources with first-hand knowledge explained that buyers use Tether, the stablecoin pegged one-to-one to the US dollar, to pay for Guyanese gold smuggled into Venezuela. The sellers receive Tether, and then they sell that Tether to Chinese merchants and traders inside Guyana, who pay them in Guyanese dollars at above-market rates. Completely bypassing the formal banking system.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: One trader estimated those transactions alone bypass the state to the tune of around 3 billion dollars annually. And this connects to a broader issue in Guyana's economy: the severe shortage of US dollars. The report highlights that international gold sales were traditionally the main conduit bringing physical greenbacks into Guyana. When the US sanctioned the Mohameds and the Bank of Guyana revoked their cambio licence, transactions through non-bank cambios plunged by nearly 13 percent in 2024, worsening the domestic foreign exchange squeeze.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: It shows how structurally entangled illicit gold trading and the formal macroeconomy really are. And meanwhile, in the mining districts, an environmental disaster continues unchecked, driven heavily by mercury smuggling.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Right. Guyana imported over 56 tonnes of mercury in 2024, primarily from India and the UAE, neither of which actually produces mercury. Miners rely on it because it's cheap, even though Guyana's natural resources minister acknowledged it threatens small miners' livelihoods if banned. And mercury gets smuggled across the border to Brazil in one-litre plastic bottles, costing around 5,000 US dollars each, fueling illegal garimpo operations.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And it poisons waterways and titled Amerindian lands, where communities are caught between armed Venezuelan sindicatos extorting camps along the Cuyuní River and Brazilian miners encroaching on their territory.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Now, let's trace this gold further downstream. Where does Guyana's legally declared gold actually end up once it leaves the country?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: In 2024, the UAE and Canada were the primary export destinations, accounting for over two-thirds of declared exports, followed by Belgium, China, Hong Kong, and the US. But if you look at the intermediate buyers, the picture gets very concentrated. After the Royal Canadian Mint ceased refining gold from the Guyana Gold Board in 2021, the GGB turned almost entirely to UAE-based commodity traders.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Notably StoneX Commodities DMCC, part of New York-headquartered StoneX Group. In 2023, StoneX became the Gold Board's sole buyer, purchasing 2.7 tonnes. And another Dubai entity, Shirpur Gold DMCC, purchased 5 tonnes that same year from private dealers like El Dorado, Mohamed's, and Pure Diamond.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: And Shirpur Gold later filed for bankruptcy and was declared insolvent by late 2025. The big systemic issue here is that commodity traders sit right between high-risk artisanal origin points and international refineries. Yet under current UAE regulations, while dealers face due diligence rules, trading companies are not required to undergo mandatory third-party audits. It creates an enormous loophole.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And refiners certified by the London Bullion Market Association, or LBMA, often rely on light due diligence when sourcing through intermediaries, assuming that if gold comes from an accredited trading hub, it's clean. The report cites a European Commission shadow audit of two LBMA-certified refineries which revealed that responsible sourcing standards were not being fully met in practice, particularly regarding intermediate refiners.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: So when you look at the entire chain, from an unregulated pit in Essequibo or Marudi Mountain, through informal cash or Tether transactions, across porous borders to Boa Vista and Caracas, or through Dubai commodity brokers into European and North American supply chains, the vulnerabilities are systemic.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: Which brings us to the recommendations. The report lays out clear, urgent steps for Guyana, international bullion hubs, and standard setters. What are the key takeaways?

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: First, inside Guyana, there must be fundamental institutional reform. The GGMC needs to modernize its cadastre, move away from first-come, first-served licensing, set strict acreage caps to end landlordism, and digitize all company records. Furthermore, all gold dealers must be legally incorporated companies subject to mandatory independent annual audits, not unincorporated sole proprietorships.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And crucially, protecting Amerindian rights by enforcing free, prior, and informed consent before any mining occurs on Indigenous lands.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: Second, the report stresses that governments shouldn't just criminalize small-scale miners. Artisanal mining provides livelihoods for tens of thousands. The goal should be upstream formalization, providing miners direct access to banking, fair finance, and mercury-free extraction so they aren't trapped by predatory middlemen.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: And third, internationally, the UAE, Switzerland, the LBMA, and major banks need to close the audit loopholes. Trading companies importing into bullion centres must undergo mandatory independent audits, and refiners must disclose the true origin and first-tier suppliers in red-flag jurisdictions like Guyana.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: As the authors conclude, closing the governance gap in Guyana is not just about recovering lost tax revenue. It is essential for regional security and the rule of law. Because as long as gold remains opaque, easily fungible, and politically protected, it will continue to serve as the ultimate financial rail for transnational crime.

turns.speaker: Daniel
turns.text: A fascinating and sobering report. Make sure to check out Following Guyanese Gold on the GI-TOC website for the full maps, data annexes, and detailed evidence. Thanks for listening.

turns.speaker: Maya
turns.text: See you next time.
